course: Brick Making Business with Bank and Mobile Money Integration
module_title: Mobile Money Integration for Brick Businesses

lessons.title: Setting Up a Mobile Money Merchant Account
lessons.body: To accept mobile money payments from customers, you need a merchant account. In most African countries, you can register with the dominant mobile money provider: M-Pesa in Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique; MTN Mobile Money in Uganda, Ghana, and Cameroon; Airtel Money in Zambia, Malawi, and Niger; Orange Money in Senegal, Mali, and CÃ´te d'Ivoire. Start by visiting an authorized agent or the provider's branch with your national ID, business registration certificate (if you have one), and a letter from your local brick makers' association. For a small brick business, you can register as a sole proprietor. The registration fee is usually between 5,000 and 20,000 shillings (or equivalent), and you may need to deposit an initial float of 50,000 to 100,000 shillings into your merchant wallet. The agent will help you set a merchant code (also called a till number or paybill). For example, M-Pesa uses a 5-digit till number for Buy Goods and Services. Once registered, you will receive a merchant SIM card and a simple phone or POS device. Train yourself and your staff on how to initiate a payment: the customer dials *182*1*1# (M-Pesa) or *165# (MTN), enters your merchant code, the amount, and their PIN. You will receive an SMS confirmation. Keep your merchant SIM in a safe place and never share your PIN. Also, link your merchant account to your bank account so you can transfer funds easily. Many providers allow automatic settlement to your bank at a small fee (e.g., 1% of the transfer). Within a week, you can start accepting digital payments, which reduces the risk of handling cash and attracts more customers.

lessons.title: Receiving Customer Payments via Mobile Money
lessons.body: Once your merchant account is active, receiving payments is straightforward. When a customer wants to pay for bricks, ask them to send money to your merchant code. For M-Pesa, they select 'Lipa na M-Pesa' then 'Buy Goods and Services', enter your till number, the amount (e.g., 15,000 KES for 500 bricks at 30 KES each), and their PIN. You will get an SMS like 'Confirmed. Ksh15,000.00 received from 2547XXXXXX on 12/5/23 at 2:30 PM. Transaction ID: QWE123.' Always verify the SMS before releasing bricks. For MTN, the customer dials *165*3# and follows prompts. If you have a smartphone, you can use the provider's merchant app (e.g., M-Pesa Business App) to see real-time transactions. For record-keeping, write down each transaction in a notebook: date, customer name, amount, and transaction ID. At the end of the day, reconcile the total mobile money received with your sales. If you have multiple employees, assign one person to handle payments and give them a unique PIN. You can also generate a QR code from your merchant app that customers can scan to pay. This is faster and reduces errors. For bulk orders, ask customers to pay a deposit (e.g., 50%) via mobile money and the balance on delivery. If a customer claims they paid but you didn't receive an SMS, check your app or dial *334# to query recent transactions. Never accept a screenshot as proof; only the SMS or app confirmation is valid. With practice, you can process a payment in under a minute.

lessons.title: Sending Payments to Suppliers and Employees
lessons.body: Mobile money is not just for receiving money; you can also pay suppliers and employees quickly and safely. For suppliers, such as clay or sand providers, you can send money directly from your merchant wallet or your personal wallet. For example, if you buy 10 tonnes of clay for 50,000 KES, you can send the amount to the supplier's mobile number. Use the 'Send Money' option: M-Pesa *334#, MTN *165*1#, Airtel *185#. You will need the supplier's phone number and name. Always confirm the number with the supplier before sending. Transaction fees for sending money are typically 1-2% of the amount (e.g., sending 50,000 KES costs about 500 KES). For employees, you can pay wages via mobile money. If you have 5 workers earning 800 KES per day, you can send each 4,000 KES at the end of the week. This reduces the risk of theft and saves time. Set up a schedule: every Friday at 5 PM, send payments. Keep a record of each transaction: date, recipient, amount, and purpose. For recurring payments, some providers offer bulk payment services (e.g., M-Pesa Business Bulk Payment) where you upload a CSV file with multiple recipients. This is useful if you have many employees. Also, you can use mobile money to pay for transport (e.g., lorry hire) and utilities. Always double-check the phone number before confirming. If you make a mistake, call the provider's customer care immediately; they may reverse the transaction if the recipient hasn't withdrawn the funds. By using mobile money for payments, you build a digital record that can help you get loans in the future.

lessons.title: Mobile Money Savings and Investment Options
lessons.body: Mobile money platforms offer savings and investment products that can help your brick business grow. For savings, many providers have a 'Savings' or 'M-Kesho' account linked to your mobile wallet. For example, M-Pesa has M-Shwari in Kenya, where you can save as little as 10 KES and earn interest (around 3-5% per year). You can lock funds for a fixed period to earn higher interest. To save, dial *334# and select 'M-Shwari', then 'Save'. You can also set up automatic savings: every day after sales, transfer 10% of your daily revenue to savings. For investments, some providers offer government securities or unit trusts via mobile. For instance, in Kenya, you can buy M-Akiba bonds via M-Pesa. In Ghana, you can invest in treasury bills via MTN Mobile Money. These typically require a minimum of 100 GHS and offer returns of 10-15% per year. Another option is to join a village savings and loan association (VSLA) that uses mobile money to pool funds. You can also invest in your own business: use mobile money to buy a brick-making machine or extra moulds. For long-term savings, consider a mobile money pension product like Mbao Pension Plan in Kenya, where you save as little as 20 KES per day. Always keep an emergency fund of at least 3 months' expenses in an accessible savings account. Avoid keeping large amounts in your mobile wallet because it may not earn interest and is vulnerable to fraud. Move excess funds to a bank or savings account regularly. With consistent saving, you can accumulate enough to expand your brick yard or buy a truck.

lessons.title: Mobile Money Loans and Overdrafts
lessons.body: Mobile money providers offer loans and overdrafts based on your transaction history. For example, M-Shwari in Kenya offers loans from 100 KES to 500,000 KES with a one-time facilitation fee of 7.5% and daily interest of 0.5% (about 180% APR). To qualify, you need to use M-Pesa regularly for at least 6 months. The loan limit grows as you save and repay on time. In Ghana, MTN offers 'MTN Qwik Loan' with limits up to 10,000 GHS. In Tanzania, Tigo offers 'Tigo Nivushe' up to 1,000,000 TZS. To access a loan, dial the provider's code (e.g., *334# for M-Shwari) and select 'Loan'. The money is deposited into your mobile wallet instantly. You can use it to buy raw materials, pay labour, or invest in equipment. Repayment is automatic: when you receive money in your wallet, the loan is deducted first. Overdrafts are also available: you can spend more than your wallet balance up to a limit, and repay with a fee. For example, M-Pesa has 'Fuliza' overdraft in Kenya, which charges 1% of the amount borrowed per day. Use loans wisely: only borrow for business needs that will generate income. Avoid borrowing to pay for personal expenses. Before taking a loan, calculate if the expected profit from the bricks covers the loan fee and interest. For instance, if you borrow 20,000 KES for 30 days, the fee is 1,500 KES (7.5%) plus daily interest, so total repayment could be around 23,000 KES. Ensure you can sell enough bricks to cover that. Always repay on time to increase your credit limit and avoid penalties. Keep a record of all loans and repayments.

lessons.title: Security and Fraud Prevention in Mobile Money
lessons.body: Mobile money fraud is common, but you can protect yourself. First, never share your PIN with anyone, not even a provider's agent or customer care. Your PIN is your signature. Second, beware of SIM swap fraud: fraudsters may call pretending to be from your provider and ask for your ID number or PIN to 'upgrade' your account. Hang up and call the official customer care line. Third, use a strong PIN (not 1234 or your birth year) and change it regularly. Fourth, when receiving payments, always check the SMS or app notification yourself; don't rely on the customer's phone screen. Fifth, for large transactions, confirm the sender's name and transaction ID. Sixth, avoid using public Wi-Fi for mobile money transactions; use your mobile data. Seventh, keep your phone and SIM safe; if you lose your phone, report to your provider immediately to block your line. Eighth, register for a mobile money account in your own name with your ID; don't use someone else's account. Ninth, be cautious of overpayment scams: a customer may send more money than agreed and ask for a refund; the original payment may be reversed later. Always wait for the transaction to settle before refunding. Tenth, educate your employees about fraud and set clear rules: only you or a trusted manager should handle mobile money. Finally, keep records of all transactions and reconcile daily. If you suspect fraud, report to the provider and local police. Many providers have a fraud hotline (e.g., M-Pesa 100 in Kenya). By following these steps, you can protect your brick business's money.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mobile Money Integration for Brick Businesses

This practical reference consolidates the operational essentials from the module Mobile Money Integration for Brick Businesses. It is written for brick producers, yard managers and small agribusiness entrepreneurs in Africa who want to move cash-heavy operations onto mobile money rails without losing control of margins, records or security. Use it as a desk reference, a training handout, or a checklist before you open a merchant account, pay a supplier, or take a loan.

Mobile money is now the default payment layer for millions of small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa. According to the GSMA State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money 2024, the region accounted for roughly 1.1 billion registered mobile money accounts and about $912 billion in transaction value in 2023, with merchant payments one of the fastest-growing use cases. For a brick business â where a single order can be a few hundred or several thousand bricks â mobile money reduces cash-handling risk, speeds up settlement, and creates a transaction trail you can use to qualify for credit.

1. Setting Up a Mobile Money Merchant Account

Most brick businesses start with a personal wallet and quickly outgrow it. Merchant accounts (also called "till," "paybill," "merchant number" or "business wallet" depending on the country and provider) separate business funds from personal funds, give you a printed or digital receipt trail, and usually reduce transaction fees at higher volumes.

To open one you will typically need: national ID or passport, business registration certificate (or a trading licence), a physical address or GPS location of the yard, and a phone number registered in the business name. In Kenya, for example, Safaricom M-PESA requires a valid business permit and ID for a Paybill or Till number; in Ghana, MTN MoMo merchant accounts require a Ghana Card and business registration; in Nigeria, providers such as OPay, PalmPay and Moniepoint require a CAC certificate and BVN.

Table 1: Typical merchant account requirements and fees in selected African markets (2024)
Country Typical Provider Key Documents Merchant Fee (indicative)
Kenya M-PESA (Safaricom) ID, business permit, KRA PIN ~0.5% or capped flat fee per transaction
Ghana MTN MoMo Ghana Card, business registration ~1% of transaction value
Nigeria OPay / Moniepoint CAC certificate, BVN, ID ~0.5%â1.5% depending on volume
Uganda MTN MoMo / Airtel Money ID, trading licence, TIN ~1%â2% of transaction value
Tanzania M-Pesa / Tigo Pesa ID, business licence, TIN ~1% of transaction value

Sources: GSMA Mobile Money Regulatory Index 2023; provider tariff pages (Safaricom, MTN, Airtel, OPay, Moniepoint) accessed 2024. Fees are indicative and change frequently â always confirm current tariffs with your provider.

2. Receiving Customer Payments via Mobile Money

Brick buyers â contractors, developers, homeowners, hardware shops â increasingly prefer mobile money because it removes the need to carry cash to a rural yard. A merchant account gives you three practical benefits:

  • Instant confirmation: the customer receives an SMS and you receive a merchant notification, which reduces disputes about "I paid" versus "I did not receive."
  • Automatic receipts: most merchant accounts can issue digital receipts, which helps with VAT and tax filing.
  • Reconciliation: a dedicated merchant number keeps business income separate from personal spending.

Practical tip: display your merchant number, QR code and USSD string clearly at the yard gate, on the delivery truck, and on invoices. For bulk orders, ask for a 50% deposit via mobile money before loading bricks, and the balance on delivery. This protects you against default and gives you working capital to buy clay and fuel.

3. Sending Payments to Suppliers and Employees

Paying suppliers and workers by mobile money is faster and safer than cash, especially when your clay supplier or casual labourers are in different towns. Use bulk payment or "send to many" features where your provider offers them. Keep a simple payment register: date, payee, phone number, amount, purpose, and the mobile money transaction code. This register becomes your evidence when applying for a loan.

Table 2: Payment method comparison for a small brick business
Method Speed Record Trail Risk Best Use
Cash Immediate Weak High (theft, loss) Small on-site purchases
Mobile Money Seconds Strong (SMS + statement) LowâMedium Customer payments, wages, supplier payments
Bank Transfer Hoursâ1 day Strong Low Large supplier invoices, tax payments
Cheque Days Medium Medium (bounced cheques) Rarely used now

Source: Compiled from GSMA Mobile Money State of the Industry 2024 and World Bank Global Findex Database 2021.

4. Mobile Money Savings and Investment Options

Many providers now offer wallet-linked savings products â M-Shwari (Kenya), MoMo Save (Ghana), M-Pesa Savings (Tanzania), and similar. Interest rates are usually modest (often 2%â6% per year), but the real value for a brick business is discipline: locking away a portion of each sale so you are not tempted to spend it on non-business items. Some providers also offer target savings for equipment (e.g., a brick moulding machine) or group savings for cooperatives.

For longer-term investment, consider treasury bills or money market funds accessed through mobile-linked investment accounts, or chama/SACCO group savings. Always compare the return against the cost of borrowing â if a mobile money loan costs 3% per month and savings earn 0.4% per month, paying down the loan is the better "investment."

5. Mobile Money Loans and Overdrafts

Mobile money transaction history is now a credit score. Providers such as M-Shwari, KCB M-Pesa, Fuliza, MoMo Loan, and Airtel Money loans use your wallet activity to offer small, short-term loans and overdrafts. For a brick business, these are useful for bridging gaps: buying clay before a big order, paying wages before a customer settles, or repairing a kiln.

However, the cost is high. Annualised interest rates on mobile money loans frequently exceed 30%â100%, and overdraft facility fees (like Fuliza's daily fee) can quietly erode margins. Rule of thumb: use mobile money credit only for short, self-liquidating needs â a loan that will be repaid by a specific confirmed order â not for long-term equipment or operating losses.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Fraud and Over-Indebtedness

Never share your mobile money PIN, OTP or merchant credentials with anyone â not even someone claiming to be from the provider. Fraudsters frequently pose as "customer care" or send fake SMS messages claiming you have received a payment. Always verify by checking your own menu or statement, not the SMS alone. Also beware of loan stacking: taking multiple mobile loans to repay each other can trap a brick business in a debt cycle. If you are already struggling, contact your provider about restructuring before taking a new loan.

6. Security and Fraud Prevention in Mobile Money

Common frauds affecting brick businesses include: fake payment SMS ("I have sent the money" when no funds arrived), SIM-swap attacks, social engineering calls, and dishonest employees who share the merchant PIN. Practical controls:

  • Verify every incoming payment in your own wallet or merchant portal before releasing bricks.
  • Use a separate merchant PIN known only to the owner or a trusted manager; change it regularly.
  • Register for transaction alerts and review statements weekly.
  • Never click links in SMS or WhatsApp claiming to be from your provider.
  • Keep a written or digital ledger of all mobile money transactions â this is your defence if a dispute arises.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Open a dedicated merchant/business wallet â do not mix with personal funds.
  2. Display your merchant number, QR code and USSD string at the yard and on invoices.
  3. Verify every customer payment in your own wallet before releasing bricks.
  4. Maintain a payment register (date, payee, phone, amount, purpose, transaction code).
  5. Use bulk payment features for wages and regular suppliers to save time and fees.
  6. Set aside a fixed percentage of each sale into a wallet savings product.
  7. Borrow only for short, confirmed orders â avoid loan stacking.
  8. Never share your PIN or OTP; review statements weekly for unauthorised transactions.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • GSMA â State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money (annual, free registration)
  • GSMA Mobile Money Programme â resources and regulatory index
  • World Bank â Global Findex Database (financial inclusion data, free)
  • ITU â Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures (mobile and digital access data)
  • Africa Business Registry â business registration guidance by country (free country guides)

This practical reference is part of the Rise Africa Skills course Brick Making Business with Bank and Mobile Money Integration. Figures, fees and product names are indicative and change frequently; always confirm current terms with your mobile money provider, bank or regulator.

quiz.q: What is the first step to accept mobile money payments from customers?
options: A) Register for a merchant account with a mobile money provider
quiz.explanation: You need a merchant account to receive mobile money payments.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common mobile money provider in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa is the dominant mobile money provider in Kenya.

quiz.q: What document is typically required to register a mobile money merchant account?
quiz.explanation: A national ID is the standard identification required.

quiz.q: What is a merchant code also known as?
quiz.explanation: Merchant codes are often called till numbers or paybills.

quiz.q: What should you do after receiving a mobile money payment SMS?
options: A) Verify the SMS before releasing goods
D) Forward it to the customer
quiz.explanation: Always verify the payment confirmation before releasing bricks.

quiz.q: How can you keep records of mobile money transactions?
options: A) Write in a notebook with date, customer, amount, and transaction ID
D) Ask the customer to remember
quiz.explanation: A notebook provides a simple and reliable record.

quiz.q: What is a QR code used for in mobile money?
options: A) To allow customers to scan and pay
quiz.explanation: QR codes enable quick scanning for payments.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer claims they paid but you didn't receive an SMS?
options: A) Check your app or dial the provider's query code
D) Give them the bricks anyway
quiz.explanation: Always verify through official channels.

quiz.q: What is a typical transaction fee for sending money via mobile money?
quiz.explanation: Fees are usually between 1% and 2%.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of paying employees via mobile money?
options: A) Reduces risk of theft and saves time
quiz.explanation: Mobile money is safer and faster than cash.

quiz.q: What is a bulk payment service used for?
options: A) Paying multiple recipients at once
quiz.explanation: Bulk payment allows sending money to many people simultaneously.

quiz.q: What should you do before sending money to a supplier?
options: A) Confirm the phone number with the supplier
quiz.explanation: Always verify the recipient's number to avoid mistakes.

quiz.q: What is M-Shwari?
options: A) A savings and loan product linked to M-Pesa
quiz.explanation: M-Shwari is a mobile savings and loan product.

quiz.q: What is the minimum saving amount in M-Shwari?
quiz.explanation: You can save as little as 10 KES.

quiz.q: What is a good savings habit for a brick business?
options: A) Transfer 10% of daily revenue to savings
C) Keep all cash in wallet
quiz.explanation: Saving a portion of daily revenue builds funds.

quiz.q: What is M-Akiba?
options: A) A government bond bought via mobile money
quiz.explanation: M-Akiba is a mobile-traded government bond in Kenya.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid keeping large amounts in your mobile wallet?
options: A) It may not earn interest and is vulnerable to fraud
C) It is the safest place
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Mobile wallets are not ideal for large savings.

quiz.q: What is a VSLA?
options: A) Village Savings and Loan Association
C) Virtual Savings and Loan Account
D) Verified Savings and Loan Association
quiz.explanation: VSLA is a community-based savings group.

quiz.q: What is the typical facilitation fee for an M-Shwari loan?
quiz.explanation: M-Shwari charges a one-time facilitation fee of 7.5%.

quiz.q: What is Fuliza?
options: A) An overdraft service on M-Pesa
C) A loan from a bank
quiz.explanation: Fuliza is an overdraft product on M-Pesa.

quiz.q: How can you qualify for a mobile money loan?
options: A) Use the service regularly for at least 6 months
quiz.explanation: Regular usage builds transaction history for loan eligibility.

quiz.q: What should you consider before taking a mobile money loan?
options: A) Whether the expected profit covers the loan fee and interest
B) The color of the loan
quiz.explanation: Ensure the loan will generate enough income to repay.

quiz.q: What is a risk of not repaying a mobile money loan on time?
options: A) Penalties and reduced credit limit
quiz.explanation: Late repayment leads to penalties and lower future limits.

quiz.q: What is SIM swap fraud?
options: A) Fraudsters trick you into giving your PIN to 'upgrade' your account
B) Swapping SIM cards for fun
quiz.explanation: Fraudsters impersonate providers to steal your PIN.

quiz.q: What should you do if you lose your phone?
options: A) Report to your provider immediately to block your line
B) Wait for it to be returned
quiz.explanation: Immediate reporting prevents unauthorized access.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using public Wi-Fi for mobile money transactions?
options: A) It is less secure and can be hacked
quiz.explanation: Public Wi-Fi can be unsecured, risking data theft.

quiz.q: What is an overpayment scam?
options: A) Customer sends more money and asks for a refund, then reverses the original payment
D) Customer pays with a fake note
quiz.explanation: The scammer exploits refunds before the payment is reversed.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect mobile money fraud?
options: A) Report to the provider and local police
quiz.explanation: Reporting helps recover funds and prevent further fraud.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for mobile money security?
options: A) Use a strong PIN and change it regularly
B) Share your PIN with employees
D) Write your PIN on your phone
quiz.explanation: A strong, private PIN is essential for security.

quiz.q: What should you do before refunding an overpayment?
options: A) Wait for the transaction to settle
quiz.explanation: Waiting ensures the original payment is not reversed.
